name: C++

facts.ai_role: The performance layer underneath the Python surface: PyTorch's libtorch, TensorFlow's core, CUDA kernels, llama.cpp, and most inference runtimes are C++.
facts.steward: ISO/IEC JTC1 SC22 WG21 standards committee

title: C++ in AI: The Performance Layer Beneath Python
answer: C++ is a compiled, general purpose language first released in 1985 and standardized today by ISO/IEC JTC1 SC22 WG21. In AI work it is the performance layer underneath the Python surface: PyTorch's libtorch, TensorFlow's core, CUDA kernels, llama.cpp and most inference runtimes are written in C++. The one thing to know before choosing it is that it buys speed and memory control at the cost of manual resource management and a steeper learning curve than Python.

sections.body: C++ is a compiled, statically typed programming language whose first release was in 1985. It is stewarded by the ISO/IEC JTC1 SC22 WG21 standards committee, and its official site is isocpp.org. Within AI it occupies the performance layer underneath the Python surface. The frameworks most practitioners import, PyTorch through libtorch and TensorFlow through its core, are C++ programs, as are CUDA kernels, llama.cpp and most inference runtimes. When a Python training script calls into a tensor operation, the arithmetic usually executes in compiled C++ or in kernels launched from it. The language therefore serves the systems layer of the AI stack rather than the experimentation layer.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The concrete AI jobs C++ does are training and inference engines, data loading and preprocessing pipelines, serving runtimes, agent tooling that must run close to hardware, and edge deployment where memory and latency budgets are tight. It is strongest where performance is the constraint: custom kernels, quantized inference, real time or embedded inference, and the internals of frameworks that other languages call. The official site's own material points in this direction, with an ISO committee study group on machine learning, SG19, meeting regularly, and with talks such as one on beating Rust at JSON serialization using reflective metaprogramming. The site does not present C++ as the language for exploratory model research, and the facts here do not claim that role for it.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: C++ has a reputation for a steep learning curve, and the official material supports that picture indirectly rather than denying it. The committee maintains a catalog of undefined behavior, and a CppCon 2026 keynote describes an initial round of memory safety hardening plus draft profiles for stronger portable memory safety guarantees targeted at C++29. Those are admissions that the language asks the programmer to understand memory, object lifetime and compilation in some depth. Prerequisites for AI work in C++ are therefore systems knowledge such as memory layout, concurrency and build tooling, alongside the mathematics that any machine learning work requires. For a beginner, isocpp.org offers standards papers, meeting minutes, survey reports and conference talk announcements, but the pages read do not describe a structured tutorial path, so a newcomer should expect to learn from books, courses and compiler documentation rather than from the official site alone.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The ecosystem around C++ in AI is large but indirect. The facts here name libtorch, TensorFlow's core, CUDA kernels, llama.cpp and most inference runtimes as C++ code, which means the libraries a developer uses are often consumed through a Python binding while being maintained as C++ projects. The official site shows an active standards community: annual global developer surveys whose results are forwarded to the committee and to tool vendors, regular mailings of standards papers, study groups including SG14 for low latency, games, embedded and financial trading and SG19 for machine learning, and in person conferences such as CppCon, with CppCon 2026 starting September 12 in Aurora, Colorado. Compiler support is visible too, with GCC 16.1 shipping C++26 reflection, contracts and safety hardening. The pages read do not list tracked repositories or a package registry, so the site itself is a standards and community hub rather than a library index.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: C++ is built for production performance rather than quick experiments. The official material emphasizes efficiency under real space and time constraints, citing industry data from SlashData and IDC on demand for programmers who can work within those limits, and the C++26 and C++29 work adds performance features such as std::simd and std::execution. The cost is that iteration is slower than in a scripting language: compilation, manual memory management and a large feature surface all add friction, and the committee is still working through undefined behavior and memory safety profiles. A team that wants to test an idea in an afternoon will usually prototype in Python and move the hot path into C++ later. The facts here do not claim C++ is unsuitable for experiments, only that its strengths lie on the performance side.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: C++ is a current standard rather than a legacy choice, and the official site supports that reading. The committee completed technical work on C++26 in March 2026 and voted the first additions into the C++29 working draft in June 2026, compilers are shipping C++26 features, and the annual survey is forwarded to vendors to inform tooling. The keynote material cites sustained growth in demand for professional programmers, especially those who know languages that operate under real space and time constraints. For someone choosing what to learn, that suggests C++ remains valuable for AI infrastructure, inference and edge roles, while the pages read do not give hiring numbers or salary data, so any claim about the size of the C++ AI job market would go beyond what the facts and the site support.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: C++ is typically used with Python rather than instead of it. The polyglot pattern is that Python orchestrates experiments, data work and training scripts, while C++ implements the kernels, runtimes and serving paths those scripts call. The facts here describe exactly this arrangement: PyTorch's libtorch, TensorFlow's core, CUDA kernels, llama.cpp and most inference runtimes are C++. On the official site, the JSON serialization talk compares C++ with Rust, and the standards work on reflection and safety profiles is partly a response to competition from newer systems languages. The pages read do not name specific Python binding libraries or framework versions, so the integration details are best confirmed in each framework's own documentation.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: C++ is weak where rapid iteration, memory safety by default and a gentle learning curve matter most. The official material acknowledges this: undefined behavior is being cataloged systematically for the first time, memory safety profiles are still drafts targeted at C++29, and modules support in GCC 16.1 remains experimental behind a flag. The language is also changing quickly, with C++26 features arriving in compilers and C++29 work already underway, which makes long lived codebases a maintenance commitment. The pages read do not say how widely the safety profiles will be adopted, when modules will be fully supported, or how C++ will fare against Rust in AI infrastructure, and the facts here do not settle those questions either.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
